items.prompt: A payments service keeps the running total of a batch job only in a local variable while it churns through a million records, planning to write the final total to disk once. If the machine crashes at record 500,000, what's left after reboot?
choices: The full running total up to record 500,000, because the OS checkpoints variables automatically
Nothing — the running total lived only in volatile memory and was never written anywhere durable, so a crash erases it completely regardless of how far along it was
Exactly half of the total, since RAM degrades gracefully rather than failing all at once
It depends on whether the variable was declared with a type annotation
items.explanation: A local variable is pure RAM. It doesn't matter whether the crash happens at record 1 or record 999,999 — nothing was ever durably written, so there's nothing for a reboot to recover. This is the volatile side of the line, full stop.
items.reference:
⚡ RAM

volatile — gone the instant power drops

💾 Disk

non-volatile — keeps its contents with no power

Why: anything that only ever touched RAM is gone the instant power is lost, regardless of how the program was designed.
items.learnMore:
Volatility is the whole distinction

RAM (including a process's own variables and the OS page cache) needs continuous power to hold its contents. The moment power stops, whatever electrical state represented your data is gone — there's no 'partial recovery' from that, it's simply erased.

Disk (spinning platters or flash cells) encodes data as a physical state — magnetic orientation or trapped charge — that persists with zero power. That's not an implementation detail, it's the entire reason disk exists as a storage tier separate from RAM: it trades speed for the one property RAM structurally cannot offer.

Every durability technique in this unit (fsync, write-ahead logging, group commit) exists purely to answer one question: has this data actually crossed from the volatile side to the non-volatile side yet?
items.reflection: Volatile vs. non-volatile isn't unique to RAM and disk — a browser tab's in-memory React state vs. localStorage, a shopping cart held only in a load balancer's session vs. one saved to a database, even a sticky note vs. a filed document all draw the same line. Where else have you seen 'fast but disappears' and 'slower but survives' coexist in the same system?

items.prompt: A logging library calls write() on every log line and treats a successful return as proof the log line is safely recorded. A crash happens one second later. What's wrong with that assumption?
choices: Nothing — write() returning without error is always a complete, physical durability guarantee
write() typically only guarantees the data reached the OS page cache (RAM); the log line can still be lost in a crash that happens before the OS flushes that page to disk
The assumption is correct only for log files specifically, not for other kinds of files
write() calls are always synchronous all the way to the physical platter on every operating system
items.explanation: This is exactly the trap: a successful write() is a claim about reaching RAM-backed page cache, not about physical durability. A crash in that gap silently drops log lines the code believed were safely recorded.
items.reference:
1️⃣ write() called
2️⃣ Data lands in the OS page cache (RAM)
3️⃣ ⏳ gap — crash here loses it
4️⃣ fsync() called → physically durable

Why: a successful write() only proves the data reached RAM-backed page cache, not disk.
items.learnMore:
write() is an optimization, not a promise

Operating systems buffer writes in the page cache so programs don't stall on slow physical I/O for every single write call. This is a genuinely good design — most writes never need to be that carefully durable, and forcing every one through to disk immediately would make normal file I/O unusably slow.

The cost of that optimization is that 'write() returned successfully' and 'this survives a crash right now' are two different claims. The kernel will eventually flush dirty pages to disk on its own schedule, but 'eventually' is exactly the window a crash can land in.

fsync() is the opt-out: it blocks the calling thread until the OS confirms the specific data is physically durable, converting 'probably fine' into 'guaranteed, as of this instant.'
items.reflection: The pattern 'the fast path only promises it reached a buffer, not the final destination' shows up far outside disks — a message queue that acks 'received' before a consumer processes it, a CDN edge that caches a response before the origin confirms it's still correct, a browser that fires a navigation event before the new page has actually rendered. Where have you seen a system's 'done' really mean 'handed off,' not 'finished'?

Because buffering in RAM is required to support files larger than a certain size

items.explanation: fsync is the entire durability guarantee for that write — removing it doesn't just make things faster, it silently converts a 'definitely safe' claim into an 'optimistic, might be lost' one.

Why: it's the one call that turns an optimistic write into a durability guarantee — at the cost of waiting for it.
items.learnMore:
Why fsync is slow on purpose

fsync() doesn't just ask the OS to eventually flush a page — it blocks the caller until the disk hardware itself reports the write is physically committed. That round trip through the OS and the disk's own write path is real, measurable latency, typically low single-digit milliseconds even on fast SSDs.

That cost isn't a bug to optimize away — it is the durability guarantee. Any system claiming both 'instant' and 'fully durable on every write' is quietly skipping one of the two, and it's worth knowing which.
items.reflection: Trading latency for a stronger guarantee isn't unique to fsync — a synchronous payment confirmation vs. an async 'we'll email you,' a blocking network round-trip for a read-your-writes guarantee vs. an eventually-consistent read, even waiting for a friend's reply before acting vs. assuming they got your message. Where else have you chosen to wait, specifically because waiting is what makes a claim trustworthy?
